newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain in uproar over leaked "dirty war" papers.
newsitem.headline: Spain in uproar over leaked "dirty war" papers.

text.p: Cries of foul play and concerns over Spanish security leaks have overshadowed charges in supposedly secret papers that the state ran death squads in the 1980s.

The uproar began on Monday when pro-conservative newspaper El Mundo published the first four of a promised 20 documents purportedly showing that the former Socialist government organised a "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels.
The complete publication on Monday and Tuesday of alleged military intelligence papers spurred calls by politicians to shut down Spain's secret service agency.

"For me, the biggest concern in this whole affair is the very serious breach of security it represents...The second in command of security fled with these papers," Secretary of State for Parliament Relations Jose Maria Michavila said on Tuesday.

El Mundo said it had obtained the papers after "intense investigative reporting" and said they clearly showed that the military intelligence agency CESID set up the death squads known as the Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL).
The GAL killed 28 people from 1983 to 1987 in a campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas.

High officials and former security chiefs in the 13-year Socialist tenure have been charged with forming GAL, allegations that contributed to the election defeat last March of former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez.

Attorney General Juan Ortiz Urculo said on Monday that the documents could provide evidence for reopening a high-level investigation of former government officials, but he said it had to be proved they were CESID papers and not court transcripts.
"We have to verify if they are authentic and if they are considered classified," he told state radio. "Each case has to be studied and re-weighed, but the road is open."
The pro-Socialist El Pais on Tuesday printed all 20 documents demanded by courts investigating the state's role in the "dirty war".

The courts have requested declassification of the documents but the government has refused, citing reasons of state security. The Supreme Court is due to rule early next year on whether the government can be forced to hand them over.

El Pais said it did not know if the documents were authentic, saying they were transcripts of what had been found during a court search of the prison cell of ex-spy Juan Alberto Perote. He claimed to have stolen them from CESID.
Perote, one of those charged in the GAL case, tried to hide the papers in the prison library and also tried to swallow some of them while his cell was being searched.
Politicians say he later sold them to ex-Banesto chairman Mario Conde who then passed them on to El Mundo, which first started publishing their contents in 1995.

Conde was formally charged in May with fraud, falsification and misappropriation of funds following a 16-month investigation into the 1993 collapse of Banco Espanol de Credito-Banesto, Spain's biggest financial crime case.

The high court decided on Monday to charge Conde's lawyer Mariano Gomez de Liano and another associate with Banesto fraud. Liano is the brother of Javier Gomez de Liano, a prominent high court judge who is trying one of the key "dirty war" cases.

Gonzalez, who denies any involvement with the GAL, told reporters on Monday there seemed to be an eerie "coincidence" in El Mundo's decision to release the potentially embarrassing papers on the same day as the latest Banesto ruling.
The timing of El Mundo's publication on Monday, after sitting on the papers for a year, triggered an uproar.
El Pais, in an editorial on Tuesday, accused Conde of using El Mundo to blackmail the government.
